questions.question: What is a database index and why is it important?
questions.title: Database Indexes — What They Are and Why They Matter
questions.direct_answer: A **database index** is a sorted data structure (usually a **B-tree**) that lets the database find rows by a column's value without scanning the whole table — like a book's index. It makes reads (`WHERE`, `JOIN`, `ORDER BY`) much faster but **slows writes** and uses extra storage.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand an index trades faster reads for slower writes/space.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Indexing everything, assuming indexes are free.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention B-tree structure, O(log n) lookups, and write/storage overhead.

sections.title: What a Database Index Is
sections.content:
A **database index** is an auxiliary, **sorted** data structure — typically a **B-tree** — that maps a column's values to the rows that contain them. Instead of a **full table scan** (reading every row), the database walks the B-tree in **O(log n)** to jump straight to matching rows. It's exactly like the index at the back of a book: you don't read every page to find a topic.

Indexes dramatically speed up `WHERE`, `JOIN`, and `ORDER BY`, but they're **not free**: every `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` must also update the index, and each index consumes storage.

sections.title: Indexes at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~sorted structure|usually a B-tree|maps value -> row|like a book index
emerald|Speeds up|~reads|WHERE lookups|JOIN matching|ORDER BY sorting
rose|Costs|~not free|slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE|extra storage|index maintenance
amber|Lookup|~O(log n)|vs O(n) full scan|huge on big tables|

sections.title: Create an index and see it help
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Indexing everything**: each index slows writes and uses space — index columns you actually filter/join on.
- **Indexing low-cardinality columns**: an index on a boolean rarely helps.
- **Function on the column**: `WHERE LOWER(email) = ...` skips a plain index.
- **Forgetting maintenance cost**: heavy-write tables pay for every extra index.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Index** = sorted structure (B-tree) for fast value lookups.
- **Avoids full table scans** — O(log n) vs O(n).
- **Speeds up** WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY.
- **Slows writes** and uses extra storage.
- **Index the columns you filter/join on**, not everything.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A database index is a separate, sorted data structure, usually a B-tree, that the database keeps alongside your table to find rows quickly by a column's value. The analogy everyone uses is the index at the back of a book: instead of reading every page to find a topic, you look it up in the index and jump straight to the right page. Without an index, finding a row by a column means a full table scan, reading every single row, which is order n. With an index, the database walks the B-tree in roughly order log n, so on a million-row table that's about twenty steps instead of a million reads. Indexes make reads much faster, which helps WHERE lookups, JOIN matching, and ORDER BY sorting. But the key thing to say in an interview is that indexes are not free. Every time you insert, update, or delete a row, the database also has to update every index on that table, so indexes slow down writes. They also take up extra storage. So the skill isn't adding indexes everywhere; it's adding them on the columns you actually filter or join on, and avoiding them on columns with very few distinct values, like a boolean, where they don't help much. You also lose the index if you wrap the column in a function in your WHERE clause.

questions.question: When should you NOT create an index on a column?
questions.title: When Not to Create an Index in SQL
questions.direct_answer: Avoid indexing when the cost outweighs the benefit: **low-cardinality** columns (few distinct values like boolean/gender), **small tables** (a scan is already fast), **write-heavy** columns (each write must update the index), and columns you **rarely filter on**. Every index slows writes and uses space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know indexes have costs and aren't always beneficial.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Indexing every column 'just in case', degrading write performance.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain cardinality and selectivity — indexes help only when they narrow results well.

sections.title: When NOT to Index
sections.content:
Indexes speed reads but cost write performance and storage, so they're a **trade-off**, not a default. Skip an index when:

- **Low cardinality** — few distinct values (boolean, status with 2 options). The index barely narrows the search, so the optimizer often ignores it.
- **Small tables** — a full scan is already fast; an index adds overhead for nothing.
- **Write-heavy columns** — each `INSERT`/`UPDATE` must maintain the index; many indexes throttle writes.
- **Rarely-filtered columns** — no query benefits, but every write still pays.

The guiding idea is **selectivity**: an index helps when it filters down to a *small* fraction of rows.

sections.title: When NOT to Index
sections.content:
rose|Low cardinality|~few distinct values|boolean, gender|index barely narrows|optimizer skips it
blue|Small tables|~scan already fast|index adds overhead|no real gain|
amber|Write-heavy|~maintenance cost|each write updates index|throttles INSERT/UPDATE|
emerald|Rarely filtered|~no read benefit|but still costs writes|drop unused indexes|

sections.title: A low-selectivity index that won't help
sections.content:
```sql
-- gender has 2 values -> low cardinality, poor selectivity
CREATE INDEX idx_gender ON users(gender);
SELECT * FROM users WHERE gender = 'M';   -- still returns ~half the table
-- the optimizer often ignores this index and scans anyway

-- a high-selectivity index that DOES help:
CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users(email);   -- email is unique -> narrows to 1 row
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'a@x.com';
```

*High selectivity (unique-ish) helps; low selectivity (few values) usually doesn't.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Indexing 'just in case'**: unused indexes only add write cost and storage.
- **Indexing low-cardinality columns**: booleans/flags rarely benefit.
- **Too many indexes on hot-write tables**: each write updates them all.
- **Never dropping stale indexes**: audit and remove ones no query uses.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Skip low-cardinality columns** (boolean, few values).
- **Skip small tables** — a scan is already cheap.
- **Be careful on write-heavy** columns/tables.
- **Don't index columns you rarely filter on.**
- **Selectivity matters** — index helps when it narrows results a lot.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Indexes are a trade-off, not a default, because they speed up reads but slow down writes and consume storage. So there are several cases where I deliberately avoid them. The first is low-cardinality columns, meaning columns with very few distinct values, like a boolean or a gender column. An index there barely narrows the search, because filtering on it still returns a large chunk of the table, so the optimizer often ignores the index and scans anyway. The second is small tables, where a full scan is already fast and an index just adds overhead and maintenance for no real benefit. The third is write-heavy columns or tables, because every insert, update, or delete has to maintain every index, so piling on indexes throttles write throughput. And the fourth is columns you rarely filter or join on; if no query benefits from the index, you're paying the write cost for nothing. The underlying concept that ties this together is selectivity: an index is worth it when it filters down to a small fraction of the rows. A unique-ish column like email has high selectivity and benefits hugely from an index, while a two-value column has low selectivity and usually doesn't. I also periodically audit and drop indexes that no query actually uses.

followup_questions: Why might the optimizer ignore an index?
How many indexes are too many on a table?

questions.question: What is a composite index and how does column order matter?
questions.title: Composite Index in SQL — Column Order Matters
questions.direct_answer: A **composite index** covers **multiple columns** in a defined order. Column **order matters** because the index is sorted left-to-right (the **leftmost-prefix rule**): an index on `(a, b)` helps queries filtering on `a`, or `a AND b`, but **not** queries filtering on `b` alone.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the leftmost-prefix rule for composite indexes.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting an index on (a, b) to help a query filtering only on b.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Order columns by equality-first then range, and by most-used-in-WHERE leftmost.

sections.title: Composite Indexes and Column Order
sections.content:
A **composite (multi-column) index** indexes several columns together in a specific **order**, e.g. `(last_name, first_name)`. The index is sorted by the first column, then by the second within each first-column value — just like a phone book sorted by last name, then first name.

This gives the **leftmost-prefix rule**: the index can serve queries that filter on a **leading prefix** of its columns — `(a)`, or `(a, b)` — but **not** `(b)` alone, because the data isn't sorted by `b` first. Choosing the right column order is the whole skill.

sections.title: Composite Index at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~multiple columns|in a fixed order|sorted left to right|like a phone book
emerald|Leftmost-prefix|~usable prefixes|(a) yes|(a,b) yes|(b) alone NO
amber|Order rule|~equality then range|=, then >/BETWEEN|most-filtered leftmost|put selective col first
rose|Mistake|~wrong order|index on (a,b)|query on b only|scans instead

sections.title: Leftmost-prefix in action
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_name ON people(last_name, first_name);

SELECT * FROM people WHERE last_name = 'Rao';                       -- uses index (prefix a)
SELECT * FROM people WHERE last_name = 'Rao' AND first_name = 'A';  -- uses index (a, b)
SELECT * FROM people WHERE first_name = 'A';                        -- does NOT use index (b alone)
```

*The index is sorted by `last_name` first, so a `first_name`-only filter can't use it.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting `(b)`-only queries to use an `(a, b)` index**: they can't — leftmost prefix only.
- **Wrong column order**: put the column used in equality/most queries first.
- **Range column too early**: a range (`>`, `BETWEEN`) on a leading column stops the index from using later columns.
- **Duplicate single-column indexes**: an `(a, b)` index already covers `(a)` — a separate `(a)` index is redundant.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Composite index** = multiple columns in a fixed order.
- **Leftmost-prefix rule**: usable for `(a)`, `(a,b)`, not `(b)` alone.
- **Order by** equality columns first, then range columns.
- **Put the most-filtered/selective column leftmost.**
- **An `(a, b)` index** also covers `(a)` queries.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A composite index, also called a multi-column index, indexes several columns together in a specific order, for example last name then first name. The crucial idea is that the index is sorted left to right: first by the leading column, then by the next column within each value of the first, just like a phone book that's sorted by last name and then first name within each last name. That sorting gives us the leftmost-prefix rule, which is the heart of the answer. The index can be used by queries that filter on a leading prefix of its columns. So an index on a and b helps a query filtering on a alone, and a query filtering on a and b together, but it cannot help a query that filters only on b, because the data isn't sorted by b first; b is only ordered within each value of a. That's why column order is the whole skill. The general guidance is to put equality columns before range columns, and to put the column you filter on most often, or the most selective one, leftmost. A subtle trap is putting a range condition on an early column, because once the index hits a range it can't effectively use the columns after it. And a nice efficiency note: an index on a and b already covers queries on a alone, so a separate single-column index on a would be redundant.

Queries starting with B or C alone do not use this index

questions.question: How do you use EXPLAIN to check if a SQL query uses an index?
questions.title: EXPLAIN in SQL — Checking Index Usage
questions.direct_answer: **EXPLAIN** (or `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`) shows the database's **query execution plan** — how it will run a query. You read it to see whether a query uses an **index** (look for `index`/`ref`/`range`) or does a **full table scan** (`ALL` in MySQL, `Seq Scan` in Postgres), then add or fix indexes accordingly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know EXPLAIN reveals the plan and how to spot index vs full scan.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Guessing at performance instead of reading the actual execution plan.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the tell-tale outputs (type=ALL, Seq Scan, rows examined) and use EXPLAIN ANALYZE for real timings.

sections.title: Using EXPLAIN to Check Index Usage
sections.content:
**`EXPLAIN`** prints the **query execution plan** — the steps the optimizer chose: which tables, which join order, and **whether an index is used**. **`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`** actually runs the query and adds real timings and row counts.

You're looking for whether the query hits an index or scans the whole table. In **MySQL**, `type = ALL` means a full table scan (bad for big tables); `ref`, `range`, `const`, or `eq_ref` mean an index is used. In **PostgreSQL**, `Seq Scan` is a full scan, while `Index Scan` / `Index Only Scan` mean the index is used.

sections.title: Reading EXPLAIN at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~the execution plan|how the query runs|join order + access type|index or scan?
rose|Full scan signs|~slow on big tables|MySQL type=ALL|Postgres Seq Scan|high rows examined
emerald|Index used signs|~good|MySQL ref/range/const|Postgres Index Scan|fewer rows
amber|EXPLAIN ANALYZE|~real run|actual timings|actual row counts|confirms estimates

sections.title: EXPLAIN before and after an index
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Guessing instead of measuring**: always confirm with EXPLAIN, not intuition.
- **Ignoring `rows` examined**: a high number signals a scan even if an index 'exists'.
- **Function on the column**: `WHERE LOWER(email)=...` shows a scan — the index is bypassed.
- **Trusting estimates only**: use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` for real execution numbers.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **EXPLAIN** shows the query execution plan.
- **`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`** runs it and gives real timings.
- **Full scan**: MySQL `type=ALL`, Postgres `Seq Scan`.
- **Index used**: MySQL `ref`/`range`/`const`, Postgres `Index Scan`.
- **Watch the `rows` examined** to judge efficiency.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: EXPLAIN is the command you use to see the database's query execution plan, which is how the optimizer intends to run your query: which tables it touches, in what order it joins them, and crucially whether it uses an index or scans the whole table. There's also EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which actually executes the query and adds real timings and real row counts, so you're not just looking at estimates. When I read the plan, I'm mainly checking the access type. In MySQL, a type of ALL means a full table scan, which is bad on a large table, whereas ref, range, const, or eq_ref mean an index is being used. In PostgreSQL, Seq Scan means a sequential full scan, while Index Scan or Index Only Scan mean the index is used. I also watch the rows column, the number of rows the database expects to examine; a huge number is a red flag that it's scanning. A typical workflow is: run EXPLAIN, see type ALL with a million rows examined, create an index on the filtered column, run EXPLAIN again, and confirm it now shows type ref with just a handful of rows. The big lesson is to measure rather than guess; and watch out for wrapping a column in a function in the WHERE clause, because EXPLAIN will show a scan since the index gets bypassed.

What is the difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE?

questions.question: What is the difference between a clustered and non-clustered index?
questions.title: Clustered vs Non-Clustered Index in SQL
questions.direct_answer: A **clustered index** determines the **physical order** of rows on disk — the table *is* the index, so there's only **one** per table (usually the primary key). A **non-clustered index** is a **separate** structure with pointers back to the rows, so you can have **many**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know a clustered index orders the actual rows while non-clustered is a separate lookup.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking a table can have multiple clustered indexes, or that all indexes are the same.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the extra lookup (bookmark/key lookup) non-clustered indexes need to fetch full rows.

sections.title: Clustered vs Non-Clustered Index
sections.content:
A **clustered index** defines the **physical storage order** of the table's rows — the leaf level of the index *is* the table data. Because rows can only be physically sorted one way, there's exactly **one clustered index per table**, typically the **primary key**.

A **non-clustered index** is a **separate** structure that stores the indexed column(s) plus a **pointer** (the clustered key or a row id) back to the actual row. You can have **many** non-clustered indexes. Looking up a non-indexed column through one needs an extra **key/bookmark lookup** to fetch the full row.

sections.title: Clustered vs Non-Clustered
sections.content:
blue|Clustered|~orders the rows|table IS the index|one per table|usually the PK
emerald|Non-clustered|~separate structure|holds key + pointer|many per table|points to the row
amber|Lookup|~extra step|non-clustered -> key lookup|to fetch other columns|covering index avoids it
rose|Trade-off|~range vs point|clustered great for ranges|non-clustered great for point lookups|

sections.title: Clustered vs Non-Clustered
sections.content:
| Aspect | Clustered | Non-Clustered |
|---|---|---|
| Stores | the actual rows (ordered) | key + pointer to row |
| Per table | exactly one | many |
| Physical order | yes (defines it) | no |
| Typical | primary key | secondary lookups |
| Extra lookup | no | yes (to fetch full row) |

sections.title: One physical order — the clustered index
Many separate structures — non-clustered indexes
sections.content:
```sql
-- a non-clustered index: separate B-tree with a pointer back to the row
CREATE INDEX idx_customer ON orders(customer_id);

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7;
-- finds matching keys in idx_customer, then does a key lookup
-- into the clustered index to fetch total, etc.
```

*Clustered = the table sorted itself; non-clustered = a side index pointing into it.*

sections.title: When to Use Which
sections.content:
The **clustered index** is usually the **primary key** and is great for range queries (rows are physically contiguous). Choose it on a column you scan by ranges or join on most.

Add **non-clustered indexes** on other columns you frequently filter or join on (e.g., `email`, `customer_id`). Make them **covering** (include the selected columns) to avoid the extra key lookup on hot queries.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Clustered** index defines the physical row order — one per table.
- **Non-clustered** is a separate structure with pointers — many per table.
- **Clustered** is usually the primary key.
- **Non-clustered** lookups may need an extra key/bookmark lookup.
- **Covering indexes** avoid that extra lookup.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A clustered index and a non-clustered index differ in where the actual row data lives. A clustered index determines the physical order of the rows on disk; in effect, the table itself is stored in the order of the clustered index, with the row data sitting at the leaf level of the index. Because rows can only be physically arranged one way, you can have only one clustered index per table, and it's typically the primary key. A non-clustered index, on the other hand, is a separate structure that stores the indexed column or columns plus a pointer back to the actual row, which is either the clustered key or a row id. Since it's separate, you can have many non-clustered indexes on a table. The practical consequence is the extra lookup: when you search a non-clustered index for a value but need other columns from the row, the database first finds the entry in the non-clustered index and then does a key or bookmark lookup into the clustered index to fetch the rest of the row. That extra step is why people create covering indexes, which include the needed columns so the query can be answered from the index alone. In terms of usage, the clustered index, usually the primary key, is excellent for range scans because the rows are physically contiguous, while non-clustered indexes are great for point lookups on other columns like email or customer id.

beats.content: A clustered index determines the physical order of rows on disk. In MySQL InnoDB, the primary key is the clustered index — rows are physically stored in primary key order. Because the data and the index are the same thing, primary key lookups are extremely fast, and range scans on the primary key are efficient because adjacent rows are stored next to each other on disk. You can only have one clustered index per table.

A non-clustered index is a separate B-tree structure that stores the indexed column values and pointers to the actual row locations. When the database uses a non-clustered index to find a row, it first navigates the index, then follows the pointer to the actual row — one extra step compared to a clustered lookup.

questions.question: When does a SQL query NOT use an index even if one exists?
questions.title: Cases Where SQL Index is Not Used
questions.direct_answer: An index can be ignored even when it exists: a **function on the column** (`WHERE YEAR(d)=2026`), a **leading wildcard** (`LIKE '%x'`), an **implicit type cast**, **low selectivity** (the optimizer decides a scan is cheaper), or an `OR` across un-indexed columns. The fix is usually to make the predicate **sargable**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know why a query skips an existing index (non-sargable predicates, selectivity).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Wrapping the indexed column in a function and wondering why the index isn't used.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Define 'sargable' and rewrite YEAR(d)=2026 as a date range.

sections.title: Why a Query Skips an Index
sections.content:
An index existing doesn't guarantee it's used. The common reasons:

- **Function/expression on the column** — `WHERE YEAR(created)=2026` or `LOWER(email)=...` makes the predicate **non-sargable** (the index is on the raw column, not the computed value).
- **Leading wildcard** — `LIKE '%term'` can't use a B-tree.
- **Implicit type cast** — comparing a string column to a number forces a conversion that bypasses the index.
- **Low selectivity** — if the filter matches a large fraction of rows, the optimizer judges a **full scan** cheaper.
- **`OR` on different columns** — may prevent a single index from being used.

The fix is to make predicates **sargable** (Search ARGument ABLE): keep the column bare on one side.

sections.title: Why Indexes Get Skipped
sections.content:
rose|Function on column|~non-sargable|YEAR(d)=2026|LOWER(email)=...|index bypassed
blue|Leading wildcard|~LIKE '%x'|B-tree unusable|prefix LIKE 'x%' is fine|
amber|Type cast|~implicit conversion|string vs number|cast hides the column|match types
emerald|Low selectivity|~optimizer choice|matches many rows|scan judged cheaper|index not worth it

sections.title: Non-sargable: function hides the column
sections.content:
```sql
-- index on created is IGNORED because YEAR() wraps the column
CREATE INDEX idx_created ON orders(created);
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE YEAR(created) = 2026;   -- full scan
```

sections.title: Sargable: keep the column bare, use a range
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created >= '2026-01-01' AND created < '2027-01-01';  -- uses idx_created
```

*Same result, but the column is untouched on the left, so the B-tree index applies.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Wrapping the column in a function**: breaks index usage — rewrite as a range.
- **Leading wildcard `LIKE '%x'`**: forces a scan — use full-text search.
- **Type mismatches**: compare same types to avoid implicit casts.
- **Assuming an index is always used**: the optimizer may choose a scan for low selectivity.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Function on the column** makes a predicate non-sargable — index skipped.
- **Leading wildcard** (`'%x'`) can't use a B-tree.
- **Implicit type casts** bypass indexes.
- **Low selectivity** → optimizer prefers a full scan.
- **Keep predicates sargable** — column bare, use ranges.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: An index existing doesn't mean a query will actually use it, and there are several common reasons it gets skipped. The biggest one is putting a function or expression on the indexed column. If I write WHERE YEAR of created equals twenty twenty-six, or WHERE LOWER of email equals something, the index is on the raw column, not on the computed value, so the predicate becomes non-sargable and the database falls back to a full scan. The fix is to rewrite it so the column stays bare on one side; instead of YEAR of created, I use a date range, created greater than or equal to January first and less than the next January first, which lets the index on created kick in. A second reason is a leading wildcard in LIKE, like percent term, which a B-tree can't use, whereas a prefix pattern like term percent is fine. A third is an implicit type cast, for example comparing a string column to a number, which forces a conversion that hides the column from the index, so I match the types. A fourth is low selectivity: if the filter matches a large fraction of the table, the optimizer may decide a full scan is actually cheaper than using the index, which is a legitimate choice. And an OR across different un-indexed columns can also prevent a single index from being used. The unifying concept is sargability, search-argument-able, meaning you keep the column untouched so the index can be applied.

beats.content: There are four common ways a query silently bypasses an index. Wrapping the indexed column in a function prevents index use — the index is built on raw column values, not computed ones. So WHERE YEAR(hire_date) equals 2024 skips the index; rewrite it as WHERE hire_date BETWEEN the two date boundaries to use it.

content: Leading wildcard in LIKE — LIKE percent-java-percent forces a full scan because the B-tree needs a known prefix to navigate
Implicit type conversion — comparing an integer column to a string value can prevent index usage in some databases
Low selectivity — if the condition matches 30 percent or more of rows, the optimizer may choose a full scan anyway

beats.content: production trap: these index bypasses are silent — the query runs, returns correct results, and gives no error. The only way to catch them is to run EXPLAIN and check whether the type column says ALL. Use EXPLAIN regularly during development on any query that runs frequently or touches large tables.
